# m12-l02 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Walking on Water.

Surface tension is the tendency of the surface of a liquid to contract to the smallest possible area.

Our big question for this lesson: how do the forces between particles in a fluid affect its behavior? Let's meet a bug that walks on water.

The water strider in Figure 7 strolls right across a pond! It can, thanks to surface tension, the tendency of a liquid's surface to shrink to the smallest possible area. Surface tension comes from cohesive forces, the attractions that like particles exert on one another.

Deep in the liquid, each particle is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbors, so there's no net force. At the surface, though, particles are pulled down and sideways but not up. That net downward force squeezes the top layer slightly, so it acts like a tightly stretched sheet, strong enough to hold up something very light, like a water strider.

## Slide 3

Beads, Drops, and Viscosity.

Viscosity is the measure of internal friction in a fluid that slows its flow.

Ever seen water beading up on a freshly waxed car? The force pulling surface particles inward makes the surface as small as possible, and the shape with the least surface for its volume is a sphere. The stronger the surface tension, the harder it is to break the surface. Liquid mercury has much stronger cohesive forces than water, so it forms round drops even on a smooth surface, while a water drop flattens out.

In real fluids, cohesive forces and collisions between molecules create internal friction. That slows the flow and turns mechanical energy into thermal energy. The measure of this internal friction is viscosity. Water isn't very viscous, but motor oil is, so it flows slowly over engine parts, coating the metal and reducing rubbing. Lava, molten rock from a volcano, is one of the most viscous fluids of all, and its viscosity depends on what it's made of and how hot it is.

## Slide 4

Adhesive Forces.

Adhesive forces are attractive forces that act between particles of different substances.

Cohesive forces act between like particles. Adhesive forces are attractions between particles of different substances. Dip a glass tube in water, and the water climbs up the outside of the tube, as in Figure 8. That's because the adhesive forces between glass and water are greater than the cohesive forces between water molecules.

Mercury is the opposite. The cohesive forces between mercury atoms beat the adhesive forces between mercury and glass. So mercury doesn't climb the tube. Its surface actually dips down around the glass.

So how do they compare? For water and glass, adhesion wins over cohesion. For mercury and glass, cohesion wins.

## Slide 5

Capillary Action.

Capillary action is the rise of a liquid in a narrow tube because adhesive forces are stronger than cohesive forces.

Put a glass tube with a tiny inner diameter into water, and the water rises inside it! Adhesion between glass and water beats cohesion between water molecules, so the water climbs until the weight of the lifted water balances the total adhesive pull.

Here's the trick. The adhesive pull depends on the length of the edge where water touches glass, which grows in step with the radius. But the weight of a water column grows with the square of the radius. So a wider tube can't lift its water as high. Water rises higher in a narrow tube than a wide one. This is capillary action. It pulls melted wax up a candle wick and water up through soil into plant roots.

Plants use these forces too. As water evaporates from leaf cells, tension pulls neighboring water molecules further into the leaf. Cohesion keeps the water from breaking into droplets, so water gets pulled the entire length of the plant, in some cases up to 115 meters!

## Slide 6

Evaporation and Evaporative Cooling.

Evaporation is the escape of the most energetic particles from the surface of a liquid.

Why does a puddle vanish on a hot, dry day? Particles in a liquid move at random speeds. If a fast one breaks through the surface, it escapes. Because of the net downward cohesive pull at the surface, only the most energetic particles make it out. That's evaporation.

Evaporation cools things off. Each time a particle with more than average kinetic energy escapes, the average kinetic energy of the ones left behind goes down. And lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature. That's why sweating cools you. Rubbing alcohol feels extra cool on your skin because its weak cohesive forces let it evaporate easily. A liquid that evaporates quickly is called volatile.

Why do humid days feel hotter than dry days at the same temperature? Humid air already holds lots of water vapor, so your sweat is less likely to evaporate. Evaporation is your body's main way of cooling, so on humid days it can't cool you as well. Think of evaporation and condensation as energy and matter flowing between the liquid and gas states together.

## Slide 7

Condensation and Fog.

Condensation is the process in which evaporated particles return to the liquid phase as their kinetic energy or temperature decreases.

Evaporated particles can come back to the liquid state when their kinetic energy, or temperature, drops. That's condensation. Bring a cold glass into a hot, humid room, and the outside quickly gets wet. Water molecules from the air hit the cold glass, lose energy, and cohesive forces hold them there so they can't escape.

The air above any body of water, like in Figure 9, holds water vapor, which is water as a gas. Cool that air, and the vapor condenses around tiny dust particles into droplets only 0.01 millimeters across. A cloud of these droplets at Earth's surface is fog, which often forms when moist air is chilled by cold ground. You can even see a brief fog when you open a fizzy drink. The sudden pressure drop cools the gas in the bottle, and its water vapor condenses.

So two changes can make water vapor condense: lowering the temperature and lowering the pressure.

So, how do the forces between particles affect a fluid's behavior? Cohesive forces create surface tension, round drops, and viscosity. Adhesive forces make liquids cling and climb in capillary action. And the pull on surface particles decides which ones evaporate, which cools what's left behind.
